# R4 — Late Galilee §4.3–4.6 (6:12–9:50; lines 6443–7506)

**Range read in full:** 6443–7506  
**Source:** Joel B. Green, *The Gospel of Luke* (NICNT, 1997)  
**Section coverage:** 4.3 Instructs disciples (6:12–49); 4.4 Compassionate ministry (7:1–50); 4.5 Good news of the kingdom (8:1–56); 4.6 Identity and discipleship (9:1–50)  
**Target slugs emphasized:** [[luke]], [[joel-green]], [[jesus]], [[peter-apostle]], [[mary-magdalene]], [[jubilee]]

## Claims

### C1 — Discipleship as preparation; prayer precedes apostles and ministry
**Locus:** 6443–6453 (slice ll. 1–11)  
**Quote:** "Luke 6:12–49 further establishes the Lukan notion of discipleship, at least in these early stages, primarily as preparation.… the connection between 6:12–16 and the rest of the chapter points to the important Lukan emphasis on prayer—in preparation not only for the choosing of the twelve apostles but also for the ministry of word and deed."  
**Claim (Green):** In Luke, naming apostles and the Sermon on the Plain both grow from Jesus’ nocturnal prayer; discipleship is undeveloped preparation more than immediate assignment. Conflict motif remains (Judas proleptically; opposition “on account of the Son of Man”) but open animosity recedes so Jesus can teach joy and enemy-love.

### C2 — Twelve: divine will, mountain theophany, new leadership vs. failed leaders
**Locus:** 6458–6469 (slice ll. 16–27)  
**Quote:** "the idea of choosing itself, the election of twelve persons, and the choice of these particular persons from among the larger group of disciples—all three are divinely sanctioned.… With scribes and Pharisees responding to Jesus with misapprehension and anger, the choosing of the twelve signals a judgment on Israel’s leadership… by inference, Jesus is establishing new leadership."  
**Claim (Green):** Mountain + emphatic prayer-to-God mark the twelve as God’s design, not narrative need. “Apostles” = authorized representatives; symbolic leadership of God’s people outweighs the minor narrative roles of most named persons. Segregation from larger discipleship has little immediate qualitative monopoly on 6:17–49 teaching.

### C3 — Peter renamed “rock”; Judas as traitor-warning from within
**Locus:** 6470–6475 (slice ll. 28–33)  
**Quote:** "Jesus’ name for Simon points toward his function and evaluates him as one who heeds Jesus’ words.… even a disciple, even one named an apostle in obedience to God’s design, can oppose God’s purpose. This brief depiction of Judas… appears as a warning to the reader."  
**Claim (Green):** Renaming of Simon as Peter links to building-on-rock obedience (6:48). Judas labeled “traitor” (not yet “betrayer”) as proleptic valuative comment; breaks any simple Pharisee-bad / disciple-good binary.

### C4 — Sermon redefines world on merciful Father; inclusio hear → act
**Locus:** 6477–6483 (slice ll. 35–41)  
**Quote:** "he undercuts the dispositions… by doing nothing less than redefining the world, positing as the foundation of this world the OT affirmation of the merciful Father (6:36)… inclusio of vv 17–19 and vv 46–49.… All are welcome, but to stay, to be able to name Jesus as 'Lord,' Jesus’ gracious invitation must be joined by obedience."  
**Claim (Green):** Against institutionalized Pharisaic/scribal sanctions, Jesus builds a new community of practices. Directed to disciples yet “in the hearing of the people” as invitation; healing/table fellowship/wide audience symbolize grace, but “Lord, Lord” without doing is empty.

### C5 — Level place: power from prayer/Spirit; crowd vs. monitor-Pharisees
**Locus:** 6485–6498 (slice ll. 43–56)  
**Quote:** "in a way reminiscent of 3:21–22 and 5:16–17, Jesus’ prayer in 6:12 solidifies his relationship to God and strengthens him for ministry.… we are to understand the 'power' that 'came out from him' as the healing work of the Holy Spirit.… They are not present to evaluate his ministry but to be its recipients."  
**Claim (Green):** Moses-typology possible but secondary to prayer→empowerment bridge. Three groups (Jesus+with-him companions; great disciples/people; unclean-spirit sufferers). Tyre/Sidon may suggest Gentile reach (echo 4:26). Diseases from unclean spirits; foe of redemptive wholeness is the devil; he healed them all.

### C6 — Beatitudes/woes: topos of transposition / reversal; not mere mimicry
**Locus:** 6501–6525 (slice ll. 59–83)  
**Quote:** "a series of beatitudes and woes embodying the topos of transposition.… the Song of Mary (1:46–55)… table fellowship (14:7–24)… rich man and Lazarus… exaltation of the crucified Jesus.… Luke, however, portrays Jesus as redefining, both now and for the eschatological future, the way the world works."  
**Claim (Green):** Reversal is structural (exact linguistic correspondence beatitude/woe) and echoes Magnificat + “good news to the poor” (4:18–19). Unlike 1 Enoch’s vindictive triumph or elite Roman altruism (Balch), Luke’s Jesus replaces common world-representations with a new order. Ascriptive (way things are), not primarily prescriptive rules—yet “anti-beatitudes” vs. conventional wisdom that wealth signals blessing (Deut 28).

### C7 — Eschatological present; no idealization of poverty; sifting audience
**Locus:** 6526–6534 (slice ll. 84–92)  
**Quote:** "Jesus’ vision of the new world is eschatological, but it is not relegated to the future.… no idealization of poverty… the kingdom of God, as a place where poverty is absent.… Even if Jesus first lifts his eyes to the disciples, then, this preamble is directed to the whole crowd… practice of sifting… (2:34; 3:17)."  
**Claim (Green):** Present-tense first/fourth pair + future middle pairs; agent of reversal is God; hope for lepers, sinners, demonized, toll collectors, women. Audience not neatly disciples-only for blessings / crowd-only for woes.

### C8 — Poor/rich as power-privilege constructs, not mere economic class
**Locus:** 6533–6535 (slice ll. 91–93)  
**Quote:** "'the poor' in Luke refers above all to those who have been marginalized… those for whom only God can bring good news.… 'rich' is not simply a declaration of economic class; it is related fundamentally to issues of power and privilege, social location as an insider, and arrogant self-security apart from God."  
**Claim (Green):** Poor/rich are socially defined constructs Jesus overturns—kingdom belongs to the poor redefines daily working assumptions. Links to Magnificat, rich fool, Lazarus, 14:12 inner-circle catalog.

### C9 — Hunger/laughter pairs; messianic banquet; honor/rejection central
**Locus:** 6536–6542 (slice ll. 94–100)  
**Quote:** "The eschatological promise of food… messianic banquet… (12:37; 13:29; 14:14–24).… this one, concerned with social acceptance and honor, is instead central to its co-text.… persecution 'on account of the Son of Man' authenticates one’s identification with God’s purpose."  
**Claim (Green):** Hungry/filled and weep/laugh map present vs. eschatological reversal (Ps 126 for positive laughter). Hate/exclusion/defamation mirrors prior challenges to disciples’ practice and Jesus’ Son of Man authority; day of opposition is joy, not moral-contract reward; prophets vs. celebrated false prophets.

### C10 — Enemy-love, porous boundaries, generalized reciprocity, merciful Father
**Locus:** 6544–6570 (slice ll. 102–128)  
**Quote:** "love of enemies is designed to mitigate social tensions… Jesus calls on his followers to form a community the boundaries of which are porous and whose primary emblematic behavior is its refusal to treat others… as though they were enemies.… rejects the balanced reciprocity and patronal ethic… posits a generalized reciprocity… roots all expected behavior firmly in the character of God (v 36)."  
**Claim (Green):** 6:27–38 continues defining new existence, not absolute demand-list. Triad love / do good / give interwoven; Golden Rule pivotal but not calculated reciprocity. Motivations: boundary-redefinition, ideal benefaction (God repays), imitation of merciful Father. Audience includes persons of means (coat, loans)—sermon interprets release/favor for narrative and Lukan readers.

### C11 — Love enemies as divine graciousness; beggars as “enemies”; cancel obligation
**Locus:** 6574–6584 (slice ll. 132–142)  
**Quote:** "'Love your enemies,' lack any commonly held ethical base and can only be understood as an admonition to conduct inspired by God’s own graciousness.… he radicalizes it by insisting that all persons should be treated as though they were close kin.… Jesus is promulgating the cessation of obligation."  
**Claim (Green):** Enemies = opponents already narrated + socially outsider beggars. “Sinners” here = closed balanced-reciprocity circles. Patronal Empire web sabotaged if God is Great Benefactor and gifts carry no debt strings.

### C12 — Children of Most High; measure running over; release without prejudging
**Locus:** 6586–6596 (slice ll. 144–154)  
**Quote:** "such behavior demonstrates that one is a child of God.… he is kind even to those who… portray themselves as his enemies.… Just as the merciful God does not predetermine who will or will not be the recipients of his kindness, so Jesus’ followers must refuse to 'judge'… By 'forgive,' Jesus means 'release'—that is, 'release from obligations.'"  
**Claim (Green):** Credit/gratitude wordplay; eschatological parentage revealed in behavior (echo John 3:7–9). Marketplace hyper-measure images God’s excess. Negative restatement of enemy-love counters Pharisee exclusion of toll collectors/sinners (5:27–32). **Jubilee/release note:** Green reads “forgive/release” as liberation from obligation cycles continuous with 4:18–19 release language.

### C13 — Finale: character and action inseparable; hear and do; rock foundation
**Locus:** 6598–6638 (slice ll. 156–196)  
**Quote:** "fundamental to Jesus’ closing remarks is the contrast between two sorts of people whose hearts are revealed in their actions.… People, like trees, are known through what they produce.… How is it that humans can be so inconsistent when it comes to their dispositions vis-à-vis the ways of God?"  
**Claim (Green):** Blind guides, speck/log hypocrisy, tree/fruit, Lord-Lord, two builders: total transformation, not bare activism. “Fully qualified” = complete training like the teacher. Proleptic rebuke of nominal lordship. Capstone: hearing without doing meets ruin; doing rooted in message relevant to final judgment.

### C14 — Chapter 7 as embodiment of Isaianic release / Nazareth program
**Locus:** 6641–6652 (slice ll. 199–210)  
**Quote:** "The message of Jesus’ deeds and words now coalesce in Luke 7, which embodies in three exemplary stories (7:1–10, 11–17, 36–50) the character of the salvation made available in Jesus’ mission.… (1) … Gentile soldier… Elisha… (2) … woman and her son… Elijah… (3) … Isa 61:1–2; 58:6… (4) … forgiveness for a sinful woman.… people can either 'acknowledge the justice of God' or 'reject God’s purpose for themselves.'"  
**Claim (Green):** Compassion (7:13) and friendship with sinners (7:34, 37) unexpected yet core. Identity negotiation intensifies: Lord, coming one, Son of Man, teacher, great prophet, friend of toll collectors and sinners.

### C15 — Centurion: reach of grace to Gentile “enemy”; Naaman echoes; faith model
**Locus:** 6654–6680 (slice ll. 212–238)  
**Quote:** "will the active presence of the good news extend even to the Gentile world?… Jesus’ failure to draw insider-outsider lines, even when faced with possible Gentile defilement… prophecy of Simeon (2:29–32) seems at the point of consummation.… 'I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.'"  
**Claim (Green):** Double delegation solves hospitality/defilement crisis. 2 Kgs 5 Naaman parallels (officer, Jewish intercession, distance healing, no face-to-face). Jewish elders argue worthiness via patronal benefaction (synagogue); centurion renounces claim and recognizes authority—elders captive to nullified world-system; Jesus acts from 6:20–38 mercy, not patronage.

### C16 — Centurion characterization; slaves, savior, distance word
**Locus:** 6684–6730 (slice ll. 242–288)  
**Quote:** "he not only regarded the slave as useful, but actually esteemed him.… regards him as a savior… As a Gentile, he did not presume to contact Jesus directly.… faith and the healing power of Jesus overcome socio-religious barriers."  
**Claim (Green):** Centurion as Gentile officer provisionally with soldiers who heeded John; second envoy via friends reframes mutuality not perpetual debt. Amazed Jesus proclaims Gentile exemplary over Israel—force reminiscent of John 3:7–9. Healing validates insight across religio-cultural distance.

### C17 — Widow of Nain: woman at center; compassion; more than Elijah
**Locus:** 6732–6762 (slice ll. 290–320)  
**Quote:** "the woman, and not her dead son, is located at the deictic center… 'healing'… should be interpreted as the restoration of this woman within her community.… Luke’s identification of Jesus as Lord… 'He had compassion for her'… Jesus speaks… directly to the corpse.… More than a prophet, Jesus is the compassionate Benefactor of the poor."  
**Claim (Green):** Male-female pair with centurion; 1 Kgs 17 echoes (only son of widow, city gate, return to mother) with variations: narrator’s “Lord,” direct speech-act vs. Elijah’s prayer-energy. “Do not weep” recalls 6:21 reverse. Crowds: fear, glorify God, “great prophet” / favorable visitation (Moses-prophet Deut 18)—correct as far as it goes but incomplete for Luke. **Jubilee/poor:** widow epitomizes poor to whom good news comes.

### C18 — John’s question: messiah redefined by Isaianic festival of salvation
**Locus:** 6764–6805 (slice ll. 322–363)  
**Quote:** "John’s interest lies on the fault line between his eschatological expectations and the realities of Jesus’ performance.… a potential disconfirmation of Jesus’ messiahship has been transformed into a redefinition of the messianic role.… 'the poor have good news brought to them'… 'blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.'"  
**Claim (Green):** Report of “all these things” = esp. Gentile benefaction + widow compassion (and wider ministry) vs. John’s judgment imagery. Answer: Isa 29/35/42/61 symphony; Isa 61:1 clearest echo of 4:18–19. “Poor” includes religious outsiders (wealthy centurion). Beatitude on non-scandal converts messianic expectations.

### C19 — John more than prophet; least in kingdom greater; justify God vs. reject purpose
**Locus:** 6807–6824 (slice ll. 365–382)  
**Quote:** "John is the end-time prophet… the Elijah figure who would forerun the coming of the Lord.… among those born of women no one is greater than John; yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.… all the people… justified God… Pharisees and the lawyers rejected God’s purpose for themselves."  
**Claim (Green):** Mal 3:1 + Exod 23:20 “before you” existentializes preparation. Kingdom inverts status measures. Narrator aside: John’s baptism metonym for whole repentance-message; refusal = refuse God’s aim. “Justify God” = legitimation of Lukan plan (executed messiah, Gentile inclusion) via repentant lives including toll collectors—not absolute stereotype of every Pharisee.

### C20 — This generation’s games; friend of sinners; Wisdom’s children
**Locus:** 6826–6856 (slice ll. 384–414)  
**Quote:** "the people of this generation call out the games, but John and Jesus refuse to play them… rejected for behaviors that are actually symptomatic of their faithfulness.… 'friend of toll collectors and sinners!'… Wisdom is vindicated by all her children."  
**Claim (Green):** Ascetic John and feasting Son of Man both branded deviant by “this generation’s” socio-religious script. Chiastic parallel: people justify God // Wisdom justified by children; Pharisees/lawyers // generation who reject. Wisdom = God/purpose; children = those aligning with purpose revealed in Jesus; “Pharisees and lawyers” can function figuratively as label for any opponents.

### C21 — Sinful woman and Simon: table fellowship, open-ended Pharisee, not stereotype
**Locus:** 6858–6874 (slice ll. 416–432)  
**Quote:** "concrete example of the irony of the popular indictment against Jesus as one who eats and drinks and is a friend of sinners… such practices… are an outgrowth and material manifestation of the ministry of salvation.… Other factors disallow the interpretation of Simon as a stereotypical Pharisee… the narrative of this episode is completed before the story has ended; we do not know how Simon responded."  
**Claim (Green):** Symposium decorum + Pharisaic purity frame. Eight reasons against reading Simon as flat rejecter (invite, prophet category, named address, teaching aim, open ending invites readers who share boundary-anxiety). Woman and Simon both deeply characterized; prior encounter with Jesus assumed.

### C22 — Woman as poor/prostitute-intruder; erotic misreading vs. faith actions
**Locus:** 6876–6892 (slice ll. 434–450)  
**Quote:** "a woman known in the city as a sinner… marks her as a prostitute by vocation… belongs to a category of persons who qualify as 'the poor'… her actions on the whole would have been regarded… as erotic.… Simon is the victim of an irony… Jesus’ status as a prophet is manifest… in his ability to overhear Simon’s interior monologue… and in his recognition of Simon as a sinner."  
**Claim (Green):** Alabaster jar does not disqualify “poor.” Polysemy of actions: conventional world (Simon) vs. Jesus’ vantage. Soliloquy marks lack of insight (pattern of opponents).

### C23 — Debt parable, hospitality shame, forgiveness→love, faith saves into community
**Locus:** 6894–6918 (slice ll. 452–476)  
**Quote:** "the connection between 'canceling debts' and 'forgiving sins' has been cultivated since… 4:18–19.… because she has been forgiven much, she loves much.… She does not need forgiveness from God, but she does need recognition of her new life and forgiveness among God’s people.… 'your faith has made you whole'… restoration to wholeness, including… restoration to the full social intercourse from which she has been excluded."  
**Claim (Green):** Creditor becomes gracious benefactor; invites Simon to rethink basis of interaction. Woman’s lavish foot-ministrations fulfill/exceed host duties Simon omitted (water, kiss, oil)—she shames the host. Forgiveness prior to scene; public affirmation for community recognition. Open ending: will Simon/table guests/readers adopt canceling-debts love? **Table fellowship** and **jubilee-release** converge: release from debt/sin and social restoration.

### C24 — 8:1–3 women patrons: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna fund ministry
**Locus:** 6921–6965 (slice ll. 479–523)  
**Quote:** "some women who had been cured of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna, the wife of Herod’s steward Chuza, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their resources.… his graciousness is mirrored in theirs.… (and not the twelve) as persons who both hear and act on the word of God (8:21)."  
**Claim (Green):** 8:1–3 heading for ch. 8: Jesus’ salvific agency; diabolic opposition; authentic response. Women + twelve “with” Jesus as companions/witnesses, not yet active proclaimers. Extraordinary for Greco-Roman world; single/widow/prostitute reach of ministry. Benefaction not debt-repayment (post 7:36–50). Service + disposition of resources; model Acts 4:32 common goods. **Mary Magdalene** first (resurrection importance); seven demons = magnitude of prior bondage. Joanna’s Herodian status mixed/dubious among peasants—not simple elite legitimation. Susanna named without further mark.

### C25 — Authentic hearing chain: seed, lamp, true family
**Locus:** 6967–7005 (slice ll. 525–563)  
**Quote:** "the three paragraphs contained in 8:4–21 develop the need for authentic hearing of the word of God.… hearing is associated with response… Those who produce fruit… are included in the family of Jesus and they are the ones who are being saved."  
**Claim (Green):** Catchwords: ears to hear; listening without understanding; pay attention how you listen; hear and do. Hearing without fruit not option; good soil = hold fast in honest heart, patient endurance. Message broadcast to crowds and disciples alike; porous boundaries.

### C26 — Sower as speech-event interpreting mixed responses; devil, testing, riches
**Locus:** 7007–7035 (slice ll. 565–593)  
**Quote:** "Jesus is represented not so much as teaching the people as interpreting what happens when he broadcasts the 'good news of the kingdom of God.'… The seed is the word of God.… the devil comes and takes away the word… time of testing fall away.… choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life… hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patient endurance."  
**Claim (Green):** Parabolic enactment of mixed reception (historiographical disclosure). Secrets of kingdom given to disciples but no private scene-shift—crowds still present; Isa 6:9–10 explains non-perception without divine predetermination against salvation. Word-of-God lineage: creation/prophets/John. Short-term faith (testing; possessions) vs. maturing fruit; women of 8:2–3 have not fallen to riches choke. Apostles still unproven competence.

### C27 — How you listen will be disclosed; kinship = hear and do word
**Locus:** 7037–7046 (slice ll. 595–604)  
**Quote:** "authentic (and inauthentic) hearing, although grounded in one’s heart, is manifest in one’s behaviors.… 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'… Kinship in the people of God is no longer grounded in physical descent… but is based on hearing and doing the word of God."  
**Claim (Green):** Lamp/hidden-disclosed: either fruit will show, or teaching is not esoteric. Physical family not rejected as outsiders nor yet exemplary (cf. Acts 1:14); catalyst to redefine family around response to Jesus’ ministry as word of God.

### C28 — Storm and Gerasa: faith over fear; Jesus rebukes as God over sea
**Locus:** 7048–7072 (slice ll. 606–630)  
**Quote:** "Where will Jesus find faith expressing itself?… he confronts these apparently natural forces as though they were demonic powers… Jesus rebukes the storm he is acting as God acts.… 'Where is your faith?'… disciples are portrayed as people who have heard the word but whose faith has not yet proven itself in testing (v 13)."  
**Claim (Green):** Parallel storm/Gerasene structure (travel, calamity detail, command chaos, calm, fear). Storm as diabolic testing for disciples. “Master, Master” grants leadership not full comprehension. Fear/amazement/who-is-this: first test failed. Continuity with 5:1–11 (Master, fear, amazement) shows little growth.

### C29 — Gerasene: Gentile liberation; Legion; commission to narrate God/Jesus
**Locus:** 7074–7183 (slice ll. 632–741)  
**Quote:** "this text concerns the crossing of boundaries in Jesus’ mission, and more particularly the offer of salvation in the Gentile world.… 'Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.' So he went away, proclaiming throughout the city how much Jesus had done for him."  
**Claim (Green):** Unclean spirit, tombs, swine = Gentile ground; first and last foray into Gentile country in Gospel. Man’s identity = bondage/release from demons; holistic healing (clothed, right mind, home, vocation). Legion power-encounter; abyss avoided via swine self-destruction. Region’s great fear rejects Jesus (not primarily economic). Denied “with him” like twelve/women; first commissioned missionary—narration = proclamation; equates God’s acts with Jesus’ acts. Proleptic of Acts power and Gentile opposition.

### C30 — Jairus and hemorrhaging woman: intercalated saving faith vs. fear
**Locus:** 7185–7240 (slice ll. 743–798)  
**Quote:** "Luke exemplifies in the most explicit form thus far the nature of 'saving faith.'… contrasts faith with fear… 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'… 'Do not fear. Only believe, and she will be saved.'"  
**Claim (Green):** Shared motifs (fall before, daughter, twelve years, impurity, touch, faith-salvation). Crowd as choking “thorns.” Woman: poor (gender, chronic impurity, medical impoverishment); touch risks contagion; public testimony completes social healing; Jesus names her “daughter” (family of God by faith not ancestry). Jairus humble synagogue ruler (not excluded by Magnificat’s leveling). Raising echoes Nain/Elijah; Peter/John/James privileged witnesses preparing 9:20. Silence order: not more miracle-attraction before mission of twelve.

### C31 — §12 Christology and discipleship mutually interpretive (9:1–50)
**Locus:** 7251–7280 (slice ll. 809–838)  
**Quote:** "one cannot embody authentic discipleship unless one perceives faithfully the nature of Jesus’ person and work; yet, one cannot adequately comprehend Jesus’ person and work apart from genuine discipleship.… The tale of the sower… introduces an apt metaphor: growth leading to harvest."  
**Claim (Green):** Transitional unit closes Galilee, stages Jerusalem journey. Contested identity: Herod’s “who,” popular John/Elijah/prophet (inadequate), Peter’s “Messiah of God” (correct as far as it goes), disciples’ “Master” (subordinate without purpose), Jesus’ suffering-vindicated Son of Man, God’s “my Son, my Chosen; listen.” Prayer settings for disclosure. Disciples now active: mission, crossbearing/child-welcome, above all listen—yet persistent imperception necessitates journey formation.

### C32 — Mission of twelve: power/authority extension; take nothing; Herod intercalation
**Locus:** 7282–7320 (slice ll. 840–878)  
**Quote:** "he called, empowers, and sends the twelve.… same power and authority are now extended to the apostles… take nothing for your journey… shake the dust off your feet as a testimony against them.… Herod… beheaded John… prospect of official hostility… Who is this about whom I hear such things?"  
**Claim (Green):** Twelve’s portfolio mirrors Jesus (exorcism, heal, proclaim kingdom, bring good news, itinerancy). Take-nothing = faith unchoked by cares/riches (8:14); depend on hospitality; stay in one house; dust as performative unclean-declaration for rejecters of visitation (not ethnic purity). Herod intercalation binds apostolic work to Jesus; John beheaded foreshadows prophetic fate. Feeding juxtaposed: empowered yet fail faith on food.

### C33 — Feeding five thousand: test of faith; kingdom benefaction; open table
**Locus:** 7322–7350 (slice ll. 880–908)  
**Quote:** "their request to send the crowd away is seen in their lack of any vocalized expectation that Jesus might be able to provide… Mary had predicted that the hungry would be filled (1:53), and Jesus had interpreted… salvation, in part, as the filling of the hungry (6:21).… No attempt has been made… to preserve the social boundaries… God’s benefaction is without limits.… twelve baskets… message of divine provision… intended for the twelve."  
**Claim (Green):** Against 9:3 no-bread/money and prior provision (5:1–11; Elisha; wilderness manna), disciples flounder. Jesus as channel of God’s Benefactor without reciprocity demand. Meal ignores purity/tithing/wash boundary-maintenance—undifferentiated mass. Apostles organize/serve (table service vocation) yet remain oblivious (→9:46–48).

### C34 — Peter’s confession: prayer-mediated messiahship; passion prediction; daily cross
**Locus:** 7352–7407 (slice ll. 910–965)  
**Quote:** "Peter answered, 'The Messiah of God.'… access to Jesus’ identity is supernaturally mediated.… 'The Son of Man must undergo great suffering… and on the third day be raised.'… 'If any want to become my followers, let them deny themselves and take up their cross daily and follow me.'"  
**Claim (Green):** Not grounded primarily in feeding miracle (no recorded disciple response; loose episodic link) but Jesus praying. Public opinions same inadequate list as Herod’s. Silence commanded because messiahship not yet integrated with requisite suffering; sanhedrin agents named. Discipleship: deny kinship-status self, daily cross metaphor (dead to world opposing God), persistent following. Life saved by losing for Jesus; possessions-forfeit language (echo 8:14); shame now → Son of Man’s glory shame then; some will see kingdom (→transfiguration).

### C35 — Transfiguration: glory, exodus, listen to Son/Chosen
**Locus:** 7409–7448 (slice ll. 967–1006)  
**Quote:** "They appeared in glory and were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.… 'This is my Son, my Chosen; listen to him!'… the apostles told no one any of the things they had seen."  
**Claim (Green):** Sight insufficient without hearing/divine word. Exodus intertext (mountain, Moses, tents, cloud, Deut 18:15) + Isaianic New Exodus; “exodus” = liberation journey through death to exaltation at Jerusalem, not mere synonym for death. Moses/Elijah legitimize continuity, not censured law/prophets. Peter’s “Master” + three dwellings = spiritual dullness (sleep) and attempt to station glory. Cloud/voice for apostles; Son + Isaianic Servant + prophet like Moses constellation. Silence until post-resurrection grasp.

### C36 — Post-transfiguration failures: faithless generation; passion hidden; greatness; outsider exorcist
**Locus:** 7450–7501 (slice ll. 1008–1059)  
**Quote:** "You faithless and perverse generation… they did not understand this saying; its meaning was concealed from them… argument… which one of them was the greatest.… 'the least among all of you is the greatest.'… 'Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you.'"  
**Claim (Green):** Four tightly bound subunits: failed exorcism (only child; pathos; disciples given power over all demons yet cannot); passion prediction II while glory-amazement still rings; status argument answered by honoring child (low status welcome = welcome Jesus = welcome Sender); John forbids successful outsider “in your name.” Fear as faith-denial; deliberative language of opponents. All twelve indicted including mountain-three. Failure establishes narrative need for 9:51+ formation journey. Boundary-keeping contradicts Jesus’ low-status welcome; unnamed exorcist fruits where disciples failed.

### C37 — Green’s social-scientific through-line: patronage, purity, honor, possessions
**Locus:** (synthetic across range; esp. 6477–6483, 6586–6596, 6694–6710, 6921–6965, 7322–7350)  
**Quote:** "If God, and not the emperor, is identified as the Great Benefactor… the politics of the Empire is sabotaged." (slice ~l. 147); women “provided for them out of their resources”; feeding without purity boundaries.
